transcription.text: Hi, I'm here with Colin Mitchell from Talking Electronics Fame. Everyone in Australia will
instantly recognize the name Colin Mitchell in this Talking Electronics Magazine. And if you
want to know, I get asked all the time where I learned electronics and how I learned electronics.
Well, this man had a big hand in it, so thank you very much, Colin.
Good, that's lovely to see you, Dave.
Talking Electronics. I learned a lot of electronics from the Talking Electronics
Magazine and we're here. Colin's going to take us through some old stuff and we're going to talk
about the history of Talking Electronics.
Now, I just want to mention this particular episode, right? Now, I didn't particularly
want to spend a lot of money on printing the magazine, having all that expense of
writing the magazine and actually laying it all out. So, I went to Electronics Australia
and I...
What date was this?
1985 is the letter I've got. And I just can't remember just how advanced I was. But the basic
concept was that I went to them and I said, look, instead of me putting out this magazine being in
competition with you, what I suggest is that I want to put in, say, 24 pages in the middle of
your magazine as a pullout section. I didn't particularly want to have advertising in it
so that the people can understand just simple projects and maybe I could back them up with a
kit because there wasn't real... there wasn't kits in those days as such.
Were Dick Smith doing kits?
No, not... no, no, he wasn't. No, no. They were probably doing a few odd kits. They had fun ways,
in fun ways and things. But they didn't really specialise in having the kit from Electronics
Australia in that month. They might have had to put in a circuit board because I went along to
Electronics and I asked him that, does he sell Electronics Australia kits? He said, oh, we don't
have any kits from them, but they do send us down printed circuit boards each month and they're
available and the people can make up the kit by going around the store making the kit. I said,
well, how many hundred kits do you sell from each of the kits per month? He said, Colin, hundreds?
He said, we get 20 boards. I said, oh, well, that's good. 20 boards from each kit and how many do you
sell? He said, come on, I'll show you. So we went upstairs in the shop, upstairs in the shop and
had a great big tray, a big tray this high, the size of a table with hundreds of printed circuit
boards on, all in plastic bags. And he said, they're the boards. I said, well, how many? He said,
maybe one or two. So I looked at them, they had no overlay on them, no legend, no
tinning, they were just bare copper. But the worst part was, is that they had no numbers or names on
them except EA4176-3024974. Who knows? Not a name on it, not even the name of the kit,
just a number. Well, how on earth could you work that out? That's crazy. That's madness. So I
realised, I learnt my lesson, never do that. So I was the first person, even in those days, to put a
legend on all the boards, to tin them, and also to put solder mask on them. Oh, solder mask was,
wow, that was... No one did it. It was all available. None of the boards did it. They were
just bare copper. So, anyway, that's going ahead of the point. Before all that, I went along to
Electronics Australia and I sent them a letter to say that I didn't particularly want to spend all
the money on a magazine. What about putting in 24 pages, a pull-out section? And I got a letter
back. This is the reign of Jim Rowe. Yes, that's right. Jim Rowe sent me a letter back.
Just sort of saying that, oh, you know, that all the costs involved in putting in these 24 pages
and things like that, and not terribly happy about it, but if you want to go ahead with it, look,
we'll consider it. He said, but on the second page, he said, but just in case you don't turn up with
the goods, the 24 pages, there will be a figure of $7,500 fine. Fine? Now, $7,500 in those days,
my car cost me $3,500. Oh, no. It was two cars. In other words, he didn't want you to do it.
That was... I wasn't prepared. So, three or four years later, he saw me. He came down and saw me.
He said, oh, you probably didn't like what I wrote in the letter. I said, I certainly didn't.
I never replied. I didn't want to have the embarrassment of replying or saying anything,
but the shock of $7,500 fine was astronomical. Oh, that's amazing. Oh, yes, because the magazine
only cost me less than $5,000 for 10,000 copies, about 40, 50 cents a copy. So, you can imagine
a $7,000 fine was a huge amount in those days. So, that's the main thing. I'm just saying this,
that there's always more than one way of doing business, always more than one way. If something
goes wrong, always say, well, you've learnt a lesson. There was a reason for that, and the
reason was I started my magazine and it succeeded. It was a huge success. I sold hundreds of thousands
of kits. I'm one of the biggest kit makers until the others came in. They saw how many kits I was
making, and then, well, Jay Carr started up again. Gary Johnson bought Jay Carr, and he did the kits,
and of course, then we've got Altonics. He started making the kits, and of course, they did. They
made Altonics Australian kits and ETI kits, and they were quite successful. So, I did have
competition, but I knew that I had my own kits, and they were totally different kits. They were
very simple kits, but we did sell many, many, I think it was about 30,000 FM bug, just of the ant.
Just of the ant?
Just of the ant, because we put the board on the magazine. It was a very cheap board, and I didn't
particularly like it, but the manufacturer had very thin paper bakelite board. Then he said, look,
I'll do the board for five cents for you, and...
Five cents?
Five cents, yes.
Wow. I always wondered, what was the motivation for putting the PCB on the front cover?
Five cents.
Five, because it was just cost.
Yes.
It was so cheap, you figured you might as well.
Yes. Well, the expensive part was sitting down and actually sticky taping them on. You know,
you could only do a few hundred an hour, and I was there every night doing a couple hundred an hour.
I had people coming around, five dollars an hour, just hours and hours of work,
with 20,000 magazines to put them on, and then, of course, we had PC boards that were stapled on.
Yes, I remember stapling ones.
And I designed the stapling machine to push the pedal, because you need an enormous amount
of pressure to push those staples, two staples at a time, and I had a very big leverage on the
actual mechanism. I had huge leverage.
So you custom-built that?
Yes.
Just for one...
We had two machines. We had two machines.
And you could re-jig it for each magazine?
No, no.
Or you could put a common tool in the hole?
That's right. The holes were always in the same place, so the magazine always fitted in the spot.
The board went on, and the two staples went down at the same time.
And we had two... we used old television cabinets to mount the staplers on.
It had two staplers on it, on each machine, and we had to have two machines,
because you had to do 20,000, and it took weeks and weeks to do it.
But another little bit of engineering that I designed those stapling machines
to staple those staples on, and they were 50 cents a board, because they were glass,
they're fiberglass.
That's right, they were fiberglass.
And they were good quality, and they had...
They had overlay. I don't think that they didn't have solder mask, though.
No, they didn't have solder mask, but they had tin. They were tinned.
Right.
They were tinned, but not solder mask, and they had an overlay on them.
And they were 50 cents a board. It was 20,000, 50 cents a board.
And who made the board?
Well, I had three different people making them. One was better than the other,
and I had different manufacturers all beating each other in the price,
but the local man, he really boomed, because it was cash,
and it was a $20,000, 20,000 a board production line.
And you can just imagine, in those days, they had quad drills,
and they could only drill, I think, three or four deep.
And four of them, so they had boards, about eight boards on a panel,
but they were quad drills, and you can imagine hundreds of holes in each one,
and just doing the same board for 20,000.
There was weeks of work, but they did it.
Yep.
They did it, and we got through, and they were a huge success.
And it started people off, because the boards from overseas,
again, the English magazine had them, no overlay on them,
no tinning, just pure copper, no identification on them at all.
It was just, I've still got the boards, because it wasn't a pleasure making them.
It was just really, the boards, they weren't a very good project anyway,
but it just wasn't worthwhile making the things,
because it just didn't finish up.
All our boards finished up beautiful,
all finished up the best you could do in those days.
So it was a huge advancement.
We did actually start a few original ideas.
The printed circuit board was one,
and the other thing was to have least or no advertising in it.
Yes, I know.
You were very, and you like to talk about that in the magazine too.
You like to tell readers about, I remember you giving stories.
Yes, because what happened is that I did a little bit of work
with one of the magazine people,
and what I particularly didn't like was that the first thing they did,
they laid all the sheets out, all the pages were all laid out on a huge table,
and the first thing that came along with the advertising people,
put all their layout all on the magazine, right?
And he turned around to me and a couple of people,
now fill the holes, and I thought that's what they treat you like.
Right.
All the editorial, all the most important material,
now fill the holes.
Now that was their attitude, and I said,
I will never, ever present that attitude to people,
that I'm just writing on the back of your ad.
Yeah.
So that's the reason why I wrote very little advertising,
because I didn't like, you're summing through Electronics Australia,
any of those magazines, and in fact what I've done is,
I've taken the hundreds of magazines I had,
which have filled up all these shelves here,
I took out all the articles, and the articles are only this high.
All the rest I put in the bin.
Now I've sorted them out all into articles,
and I've almost, probably four metres high,
finished up that much worth of articles.
Fantastic.
How did you produce the magazine back in those days?
Because there was no computer.
So it was all just literally you would...
On a typewriter.
On a typewriter, yep.
We'll call it an electronic typewriter, it had a memory in it.
And it was all hand done, all stuck down,
every little tiny thing was all...
Stuck down with glue?
That horrible cow gum.
But of course the cow gum makes all the paper brown.
Right, yep.
And so all the artwork I've got now is absolutely worthless.
It's ruined.
It's all brown, it's as brown as a berry now.
And even though the pieces have all stuck down,
some of those circuit diagrams would have had over a hundred little stick downs,
because everything had to be stuck down, all letrasetted.
Yep.
Because letraset was very expensive.
So we finished up typing out all those different symbols
and just sticking them down as separate items.
But that's all we had.
Wow.
And that's why you hand drew a lot of...
You hand wrote a lot of your 10-minute digital...
Well, that was another concept.
On that grid idea, that was another concept.
I had seen it somewhere else and the other person said,
oh, you copied me.
I said, well, of course I copied you.
Who was that?
That was the man from America.
Oh, Forrest Mimms.
Yes, that's right.
It was copied from him.
Engineer's Mini Notebooks.
That's right.
That's right.
So that I had the...
It was hardly original, though.
Oh, no.
His was original, but I got a hundred sheets printed
with a very grey background, grey stipple,
and with a blackboard around.
I got a hundred sheets printed.
And of course, when you write on, you can't afford to make a mistake,
because any whiteout is showing.
Yeah, it shows out.
So you're very careful to write to the page.
It was a lot of work.
Did you draft them first, by draft?
No, I didn't.
No, you just sat down and carefully thought about it?
That's right.
And worked it out to the page.
And it takes a lot of time, because you had to do it all by hand
with a very fine tip pen.
You couldn't make a mistake, and you had to think about it.
But it was very successful.
It was another concept of teaching someone,
because some people are visual.
Some people want to see diagrams and drawings.
And of course, now that we've got videos,
that's going to teach a lot more people.
Because a lot of electronics people
may not be able to work out the square root of minus four,
but they can certainly make a project.
Absolutely.
And they can solder, and they can think.
Yeah.
So that people have a certain ability.
So you've got to cotton onto that ability and say,
look, once you learn electronics, you're made.
You are absolutely made.
Because you can go into servicing, design.
You can go into so many areas.
And you don't have to be a brilliant engineer.
You don't have to even be able to know the English language.
But electronics is a different field.
Well, it's a practical field.
As long as you can build something,
and possibly reproduce it.
It's something we can't put our finger on.
Yep.
Because some of the cleverest people that I've had
are just the average person that has come along,
but absolutely brilliant electronics,
but only did very average in school.
Yep.
So they're the people that we're trying to encourage.
And with videos, and all these different areas.
And then sometimes these people click,
and they say, hey, that's for me.
And the younger you get, it's wonderful.
But whatever the age is, if you can just click on electronics,
you can make it and become successful.
And that's what we're all here for.
That's why we've got all these different areas,
and videos, and the internet.
And all these different areas that people
can just pick up on electronics.
Do you have any idea of what your demographics were
back in the heyday?
What age groups?
People, was it mainly kids?
Young people.
It was mainly kids.
Yes, that's right.
Yep.
You saw the magazine in the newsagent.
Because this is before the internet kiddies.
Yes.
That's right.
We didn't, you know, you went into the newsagent.
My idea is to get the person very, very young,
and bring them up to that level.
That's the level that's never covered
by any of the institutions,
never covered by the universities,
or any of the technical schools.
They all want you to know something,
or they teach you far too much mathematics.
And then it slows you down.
You think, all this math, you don't need it.
If you want to do something, put the resistors in.
Put them in parallel.
Measure it.
Exactly.
And you find that you'd spend 10 minutes
working out the value,
and only a fraction of a second to measure on a meter.
I know.
Why learn if resistors in parallel?
Why learn triple calculus, and Maxwell's equations,
and everything else?
You know, okay, it's wonderful to be able
to have that ability.
But I'm just saying, you can get through without it.
You can get through with just using test equipment,
and you can do amazing things
with the simplest of test equipment.
Absolutely.
So you don't need expensive things.
You can do it with experimentation,
and developing things.
So that was my area, to just teach people,
just to bring them up without expensive equipment,
and complicated circuit diagrams,
just to teach them the basics.
And it was a huge success,
because we were one of the biggest kit suppliers.
Hundreds of thousands of kits.
That's right.
Very successful.
How many copies of each issue did you produce?
Well, what happened is that we printed 20,000.
You see, what happened is that
I went to Electronics Australia,
and I said, well, how many copies do you sell?
And they said, our readership is 72,000.
So I thought, oh, well, if that's 72,000,
I'll just print 20 or 25,000, and see how it goes.
So we sold, out of the 25,000, we sold about 14,000.
And I thought, well, that was fair enough,
because I'm only dealing with a very small area.
No amateurs, none of the people in audio.
There's a whole lot of areas that we didn't cover.
It didn't cover the high technicians, things like that.
Then I had a few magazines out,
and then I found the truth with Electronics Australia.
When they say 72,000 were their readership,
they multiply the sold copies by 2.3.
Why 2.3?
That was just the way they did it.
Just the magic number.
That's right.
So that when they were trying to sell advertising,
they said our readership is 72,000.
So divide 72,000 by 2.3, so that's less than half.
So that's 30,000.
You won't be surprised to know I've learnt the same thing
once I've got into this business,
and advertising and everything else.
It's still going on today in the electronic magazines.
Yes, lies and deception.
It is.
That's right.
Yep.
So that's the reason why I only tell the truth.
It's absolutely pointless.
And readership is a pointless figure.
How many sold copies?
I sold about 14,000.
So what happened is that the other 6,000 or 8,000 that weren't sold,
I'd got about 3,000 or 4,000 back.
I had to pay for them five cents a copy,
but they said the other ones were lost.
I know they were sold and I didn't get it.
Right.
So that was why the newsagents make a fortune,
because they normally get 25%,
they get 100% when they say that they haven't sold it,
but don't return it.
Have you ever seen a newsagent go under?
They don't, because they're living off all the magazines.
So I got back about 60,000 or 70,000
by the time I'd done a lot of magazines and a lot of other ones.
So what I decided to do,
I decided to put them into packs of two and three.
Now I remember that.
Yep, you sold them off.
And we sold them again to the people for a few dollars for three magazines,
so that every single magazine was sold.
We didn't waste any.
Yep.
So we printed about 20,000 multiplied by about 25 different issues
and some of them were reprinted again.
So overall, I think there was about between 500 to 700,000 copies
were actually sold,
because even the ones that were stolen from the shop,
they were still sold copies.
Somebody got them in the finish,
because the newsagent just couldn't account for them.
So that was a huge success there.
Did you find that your readership increased?
No, it pretty much was constant from day one.
Yes, that's right.
It didn't change.
Yes, it didn't change.
So after about the died for 10th issue,
somebody said to put color on the cover.
So on the 10th issue for the...
That's right.
You changed the color.
That's right.
So we put four color cover.
Yep.
Four color.
How much extra did that cost?
Two or three thousand dollars more.
You had to get separations
and it was a four color machine instead of a two color machine.
All right.
So it cost quite a few thousand dollars more.
Do you know it didn't increase the sales?
Really?
Yes.
We only did it for one or two times,
and then we went back to two color.
Right.
It didn't change.
I just wanted to prove to people that...
Electronics people are not interested in color.
No, content.
That's right.
It's all about the content.
So the wonderful thing we get now from Silicon Chip,
that is the top magazine in the world.
Yep.
The color,
the quality of the paper,
the articles.
In fact, EPA, the English magazine,
is just stealing the content,
whole as bowlers.
Oh, and there's a licensing agreement between the two.
That's right.
Yeah.
Just stealing it, whole as bowlers.
It's all Jim's Row and it's all 10-year-old stuff.
That's all going in there.
It's directly inserted.
And it's improved their magazine considerably.
Exactly.
But England did have a very good magazine,
Macklin Magazine.
Macklin, that's right.
It was all color.
They couldn't keep it up because it was too expensive.
The overheads were too much.
Right.
How many magazines were there in Australia back in the peak?
Five.
Five.
There was Elektor.
Elektor.
That wasn't Australian though.
Yes, it was.
Was it?
Yes.
They did in Australia.
Yes, Hans Mouse.
Hans...
He brought it here.
Right.
Oh, okay.
Hans brought it here for four or five issues.
Oh, okay.
He got the license and he reprinted it here slightly.
I don't remember seeing it in my newsagents.
Right, only for a few months.
Right.
Then there was ETI.
Yes.
Then there was Electronics Australia.
Yep.
Then there was Hobby Projects.
Oh, was that a separate one?
That was the competition to me.
What happened is that when I brought my magazine out,
it would only just start to come out.
I don't know whether I got the first issue out or not.
But Electronics Australia found out about it.
And it was Colin Rivers found out about the magazine.
And he sent all his men around to all the electronics shops
to sell them half price advertising for 12 months.
Oh, no.
So that when I sent my man around, I sent Bill around there,
he got to the third shop in the city there
and he rang me up and said,
Electronics Australia, ETI International has been around
and has sold them all advertising for 12 months at half price.
And they've got no money left over for anything else.
I said, don't worry, Bill, come back and I'll cut the advertisement.
I won't put any advertising at all
and we'll continue on with no advertising at all.
So that's what happened there.
Right.
Then what they did is they brought their magazine,
Hobby Electronics in with Phil Waite
and various other different people.
Oh, okay.
Yes, I remember the name.
And mine was $1.25 or $1.20, $1.25.
They brought theirs in for 95 cents.
Then they started with 30,000.
Then they brought in there, they brought next time 40,000.
Wow.
Then they started it with 50,000.
Then after six months, Colin Rivers rang me up
and I remember I was sitting in the room,
the phone rang and said, Colin Rivers here.
And he said, you've won the day.
And I said, what do you mean?
He said, oh, well, we're pulled out.
Yep.
With the magazine, it cost us $40,000 or $50,000.
And...
They were running at a loss, were they, or?
Obviously they were.
They had very little advertising in it,
but they wanted to knock me
because they just didn't want the competition.
I said, it's made no difference to me.
I still sell my 10,000 to 14,000.
It's made no difference to me
because I knew that it was competition
and they wanted to knock that
because there's only ETI in Electronics Australia.
Was there Australian Electronics Monthly back then?
Yes, that was taken off.
That was another one.
That was taken from the man who had a son
as well in Electronics.
He...
Yes, he had a son.
He did a lot of writing for the magazine
and that was a takeoff
because one of the...
He left somewhere else
and he started Australian Electronics Monthly
from ETI or...
Oh, Roger Harrison.
Roger Harrison, I think.
Could be, he had a son.
Anyway, he had a son.
He wrote a few articles as well.
So that...
And Silicon Chip, of course,
left Electronics Australia.
Yes, that was about 87, was it?
I don't remember.
Late 80s?
Yes.
That's right.
And that was all full colour
because that's been a huge success.
And of course, that was the one
that really killed Electronics Australia
and killed ETI
and killed Australian Electronics Monthly,
whatever, it changed its name.
Well, Federal Publishing killed it.
They tried to turn it
into a glossy consumer magazine.
Oh, did they?
And all the customers...
Oh, yes, that's right, yes.
And they cut out all the technical articles
and all the hobby things.
All hobby stuff was gone
and it was just CD player reviews
and all sorts of stuff.
And it lasted about five issues or something
and then it just died, so...
No, Silicon Chip is brilliant.
It is absolutely top quality
for a tiny country like Australia.
I know.
They were very successful.
Those notebooks were very successful.
The Engineers and Electronics notebooks,
starting with TTL, there we go.
And these are all hand...
Some of the pages were hand done.
Some of the pages were hand drawn.
There we go, all hand drawn stuff.
Fantastic.
And then you just photo-reduced these, obviously.
They were reduced too much.
They were reduced to 50%, it was too much.
You can only reduce something to 70%.
It's still readable.
Okay, and it wasn't readable.
No, yes, that's right.
And they don't produce magazines like this anymore.
It's all computer, desktop publishing.
When did the desktop publishing thing start, Dionne?
Oh, well, my first one was about $3,000 or $4,000
of electronic typewriter
and it was called Justify,
so that you type it all out
and then you push the button
and it would justify it.
It would justify it for you.
It all came out columns, it was parallel columns.
And it had a huge memory in the back there
to remember all this because in those days
the cards were only a few K, you know.
Yeah, yeah, exactly.
Only a few K.
K, that's a couple of pages, right?
That's all it was.
Well, it needed quite a few K just to produce a page.
Page, okay, yep.
That's right.
So it had all this memory in the back,
I had to pay thousands of dollars extra for memory
and I bought a 300 DPI laser printer.
Ooh, okay.
It was a Canon laser printer, which was thousands of dollars
and I bought Adobe font on it, which was another $1,200.
Just for the font cartridge.
For the font that went into the machine.
So the whole thing was very expensive.
I think my first computer was about $12,000 or $14,000.
Wow.
For the computer, the hard drive, the tower, the keyboard
and quite a few thousand dollars for the 300 DPI printer.
Yep.
Now, 300 DPI is not good enough.
Yep.
Then I bought for a quarter of the price,
I bought a 600 DPI and it was quite readable, quite readable.
Much, much better.
So from then on, I produced the magazines on 600 DPI.
Yep.
And the last magazines were all,
and you can't tell the difference between photo typeset and 600 DPI.
Okay.
Talking electronics, when,
how many people did you have working for you at the peak of the...
Once I was at eight.
Eight?
And you were still working from home?
Yes.
35 rows, one over the other?
I built on the back.
Oh, you built on the back?
Yes, I built, yes, I built on the back.
And you had eight people working there on site?
Well, yes, because I had two people in one room,
two people in another room,
two people in another room and two people in the lounge room.
Right.
And I had...
Okay, so the house was fully occupied as a workspace?
Yes, that's right, yes.
Right.
Yes.
Oh, brilliant.
I had quite a few rooms in the house.
Yep.
I built on, it's all a separate area at the back there,
I built on and more different rooms, yes.
Excellent.
How long did that last, that sort of the peak period?
Oh, it was only a year, two years.
Only a couple of years?
Yes, that's right.
It seems to me to be much longer than that from my memory.
No, there was a peak, you see, you see the peak?
Yep, yep, okay.
It built up and up and up to only two years of peak
and then just faded away again.
But it was always a mail order business from home, wasn't it?
Well, I did.
I had three inputs.
I had people coming.
Now, what happened is that I employed one boy who stole some things.
Right.
So that we dismissed him on the spot.
Of course, his father was furious, rang up the local council
and, of course, claimed that I'm working for premises at the back of the house,
which is illegal.
I said, well, is it illegal?
They said, oh yes, it's illegal to run a shop at the back.
I said, well, what's the definition of a shop?
He said, well, you've got things on display.
I said, no, that's not a definition of a shop.
The definition of a shop is it's got a cash register.
Oh, right.
I said, we don't have a cash register.
There you go.
So it's not a shop.
So that was the legal definition.
That's right.
That's how you got around it.
Yes, because you can have things sitting out there because we're an assembly place.
Yep.
And he said, well, you're big.
